title: Trend Surface Analysis and Seismic Stratigraphy of the Virginia Coast Reserve
text:
What it is
Sediment grain-size, organic-matter, and stratigraphic data from vibracores, interpreted together with high-resolution seismic records to reconstruct the pre-transgression landscape and Holocene/Pleistocene boundary on the Virginia Coast Reserve (Hog Island Bay area).

title: Trend Surface Analysis and Seismic Stratigraphy of the Virginia Coast Reserve
text:
Explanation of data
The big idea. The coast of Virginia is a landscape of barrier islands, marshes and shallow bays. Over thousands of years the sea has risen and the land has shifted. Under the bay floor, layers of sediment record that history, like the layers of a cake. Studying those layers is called stratigraphy. This dataset combines sediment cores taken near Hog Island Bay with seismic information, to reconstruct what the land looked like before the sea flooded it.
Time words. Two geologic time words appear in the README:

Pleistocene: the older geologic period (the last “ice ages”), when sea level was generally lower and this area was land.
Holocene: the younger period that began about 11,700 years ago and includes today.

The Holocene/Pleistocene boundary is the surface where younger sediments sit on top of older ones. It is a map of the old landscape that was drowned. The README also lists a 300 YBP surface, where YBP means years before present (a surface dated to about 300 years ago; see the metadata for how it is defined). Transgression means the sea moving landward as sea level rises.



A cartoon of seismic reflection: sound pulses travel through water and sediment, echoes return from boundaries, and a vibracore sample checks the layers.


Cores. The README says the data come from vibracores: a long tube is vibrated down into soft sediment and pulled out, giving a column you can look at layer by layer. The README says the cores were collected prior to 1997. From the cores you get:

Grain size: how big the particles are, from coarse sand to fine silt and clay. Grain size tells you about the energy of the water that deposited the sediment: fast water leaves coarse grains, calm water leaves fine ones.
Organic-matter content: how much of the sediment is made of once-living material, such as marsh plants.

Seismic reflection. The README says the core data are interpreted together with high-resolution seismic records. In a seismic-reflection survey, a boat sends sound pulses down through the water and the sediment. When the sound reaches a boundary between layers that differ in density or stiffness, part of it is reflected back to a receiver. How long the echo takes to return tells you how deep the boundary is. Cores are used to check what the layers really are. The README says the seismic information is described in associated publications, so the dataset itself may not contain raw seismic records. Check what is actually in the data tables.
Trend surface analysis. The title includes trend surface analysis, a statistical method that fits a smooth surface (like a gently tilted sheet) through scattered measurements, here to show how the depth of a boundary varies across the area. It is a way to map a surface from points. The README also suggests paleotopography, the shape of the land surface in the past.
Expect different kinds of data. This dataset mixes core measurements (grain size, organic matter) with horizon data (depths of the 300 YBP and Holocene/Pleistocene surfaces) and probably location columns. The README does not give the units, so check the metadata.






Not stated in the README: column names, units, number of cores and how horizon depths are measured. Check the metadata page.

title: Bonanza Creek LTER: Borehole Temperature Data from Permafrost Site near Fairbanks, Alaska (2009–2021)
text:
What it is
Temperature profiles from deep boreholes (40–75 m) in permafrost near Fairbanks, Alaska. Part of long-term monitoring of the active layer and permafrost thermal regime.

title: Bonanza Creek LTER: Borehole Temperature Data from Permafrost Site near Fairbanks, Alaska (2009–2021)
text:
Explanation of data
The big idea. In cold regions like Interior Alaska, the ground can stay frozen for years. Permafrost is ground (soil, rock or ice) that stays at or below 0 °C for at least two years in a row. Above it is the active layer, the top layer of ground that thaws in summer and refreezes in winter. Permafrost matters because thawing can change the landscape, release stored carbon, and damage roads and buildings.



Left: a ground column with an active layer on top, permafrost below and a borehole with sensors. Right: a schematic temperature profile where summer and winter curves converge with depth.


What is a borehole? A borehole is a narrow hole drilled into the ground. Here, temperature sensors are placed at several depths down the hole, so that you can measure how temperature changes with depth over time. The README says these boreholes are 40–75 m deep, near Fairbanks, Alaska, and that the record runs from 2009 to 2021. It also includes surface temperature data, so you can compare the top of the ground to the deep ground.
Why measure temperature in the ground? Heat from the surface slowly soaks downward. The yearly warm and cold swings are large near the surface and get smaller with depth, like ripples fading as they spread across a pond. Deep down, the temperature changes very slowly, so it is a sensitive record of long-term warming. This is why the README suggests comparing surface and deep temperatures and looking at long-term warming trends.
Temperature profile. A profile is temperature plotted against depth at one moment (or averaged over a period). The 0 °C line is important: ground colder than 0 °C is frozen, and ground warmer than 0 °C is thawed. (Salty or fine-grained soils can freeze or thaw slightly away from 0 °C, which is a detail you can ignore for this project.)
Active-layer thickness and thaw depth. The README suggests estimating thaw depth or active-layer thickness, which means how deep the 0 °C line moves down in summer. With sensors at only certain depths, you would estimate this by looking at where the temperature crosses 0 °C between sensors, so explain your method.
Mind the sites and sensors. The README says the sites span a range of permafrost and environmental conditions, so compare sites carefully. It does not state the units (temperature is almost certainly in degrees Celsius, but verify), the sensor depths or the measurement frequency.

title: MacroSheds Watershed Synthesis (also listed under Biogeochemistry)
text:
Explanation of data
This page covers the same dataset as the Biogeochemistry MacroSheds page, which has the full explanation of solutes, concentration and load. Here is the short version for a water-focused project.
The big idea. A watershed is all of the land that drains to one point on a stream. MacroSheds combines daily measurements from more than 200 small watersheds across the United States, with consistent formatting (harmonized) so you can compare them.
What matters most for hydrology?

Discharge (streamflow): how much water flows past a point in the stream per unit of time (daily in this dataset).
Precipitation: rain and snow falling on the watershed, where available.
Watershed attributes: climate, geology, terrain, vegetation and land cover, which help explain why watersheds behave differently.

Runoff generation. The README suggests studying controls on runoff generation. Runoff is the part of precipitation that ends up in the stream. A watershed’s water budget shows where rain goes: P = Q + ET + ΔS. Precipitation (P) leaves as streamflow (Q) and evapotranspiration (ET, water returned to the air by evaporation and plants), or is held back as a change in storage (ΔS, in soil, groundwater and snow). Comparing Q to P across watersheds, and relating that to attributes like climate, vegetation and terrain, is a natural project.



A watershed water budget: P = Q + ET + ΔS.


Integration with chemistry. The dataset also has stream chemistry, so you can ask how flow and chemistry are linked. A concentration (dissolved amount per volume of water) combined with discharge gives a load (how much leaves per time). See the Biogeochemistry page for details.






Not stated in the README: units, which sites have precipitation, and how long each record is. Check the metadata page, the dashboard or the R package.

title: Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest: Daily Streamflow by Watershed, 1956–present
text:
What it is
Continuous daily streamflow records from nine small watersheds (12–77 ha) at the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest in New Hampshire. One of the longest continuous watershed hydrology records in the United States.

title: Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest: Daily Streamflow by Watershed, 1956–present
text:
Explanation of data
The big idea. A watershed is all of the land that drains to one point on a stream, like a bowl that funnels rain to a single drain. This dataset records how much water leaves nine small watersheds (12–77 hectares each; a hectare is about the size of a soccer field) at the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest in New Hampshire, every day since 1956. It is one of the longest watershed records in the United States.
What is streamflow? Streamflow (also called discharge) is how much water flows past a point on a stream. For small watersheds like these, flow is commonly measured at the outlet with a gauge on a small dam called a weir. A sensor records how high the water is (the stage), and that height is converted to flow. (The README does not describe the instruments in detail, so check the metadata.)



A weir: stage (water level) behind a small dam is converted to discharge.


Units: mm/day. The README gives streamflow in millimeters per day. That may look odd for a flow, but it is clever: it is the volume of water divided by the watershed’s area, so it is the depth of water that would cover the whole watershed. That makes a 12-hectare watershed directly comparable with a 77-hectare one.
The water budget. Where does rain go? A watershed’s water budget says: P = Q + ET + ΔS.

P (precipitation): rain and snow that fall.
Q (streamflow): water that leaves in the stream. This is the variable in this dataset.
ET (evapotranspiration): water that returns to the air by evaporation and by transpiration (plants releasing water vapor through their leaves).
ΔS (change in storage): the change in water held in soil, groundwater and snow.

Over many years, storage changes little, so rain is roughly split between streamflow and ET. This dataset only has Q. It does not include P or ET, so you need other data to close the budget.



A watershed water budget: P = Q + ET + ΔS.


Reference vs. experimental watersheds. The README says some watersheds are reference (left alone, as a baseline) and some were experimentally manipulated. Its suggested analyses mention deforestation experiments such as clear-cutting. Trees pump a lot of water back to the air, so one idea you could test is whether cutting trees changes streamflow. Compare treated watersheds with reference watersheds, and look at the data rather than assuming the answer.
A caution on the instruments. The README notes a transition from chart-recorder to digital sensors. A change in equipment can change how data look, so check whether a jump in your data lines up with that transition.






Not stated in the README: which watersheds are reference or treated, and when each treatment took place. Check the metadata page.

title: Climate Data from Niwot Ridge LTER D1 Station (High-Elevation Alpine)
text:
What it is
High-frequency (10-minute) climatological data from the D1 climate station on Niwot Ridge, Colorado (elevation ~3738 m). Part of the Niwot Ridge LTER long-term monitoring program.

title: Climate Data from Niwot Ridge LTER D1 Station (High-Elevation Alpine)
text:
Explanation of data
The big idea. Niwot Ridge is in the Colorado Front Range, and the D1 station sits at about 3,738 m (roughly 12,300 ft) above sea level. That is an alpine site: very high in the mountains, where it is cold, windy and sunny and the weather can change quickly. The station is part of the Niwot Ridge LTER (Long Term Ecological Research) monitoring program.
What was measured? The README lists:

Air temperature and relative humidity (water vapor in the air compared with the most the air could hold at that temperature).
Wind speed and direction. By meteorology’s usual convention, direction is where the wind blows from; confirm in the metadata.
Solar radiation: the energy arriving from the sun.

The README also says the data are quality-flagged and at native resolution. A flag is a code next to a value saying that it is good, estimated or suspicious. Native resolution means the data have not been averaged: you get a record every 10 minutes. That is dense data: there are 144 records per day per variable.
What does 10-minute data let you do? Because values are so frequent, you can see the diurnal cycle, a pattern that repeats every 24 hours (temperature usually climbs after sunrise and falls overnight). You can also look at seasonal cycles across the year, extreme wind or temperature events, and how fast conditions change. Before you plot, check the flags and decide how to treat flagged values, and think about whether to average to hourly or daily data so graphs are readable.
Why elevation matters. High-elevation stations are generally colder and windier than low ones, which is why the README suggests comparing D1 with lower-elevation stations. That comparison needs data from another source, so check that it is available before choosing it.






Not stated in the README: exact variable names, units and flag codes, and whether other variables (such as precipitation or snow) are included. Check the metadata page.

What it is
Paired measurements of methane (CH₄) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) fluxes and soil biogeochemical properties from a tidal salt marsh and an impounded brackish wetland in Georgetown County, South Carolina (2022–2023).

title: Chamber-Level Gas Fluxes and Soil Biogeochemical Properties from Coastal Wetlands, South Carolina
text:
Explanation of data
The big idea. Wetland soils hold a lot of carbon, and they can release two greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide (CO₂) and methane (CH₄). This dataset pairs measurements of those gas fluxes with measurements of the soil beneath, so you can ask why some spots release more gas than others. The data come from two kinds of coastal wetland in Georgetown County, South Carolina, measured about monthly in 2022–2023: a tidal salt marsh and an impounded brackish wetland.

Tidal salt marsh: flooded by ocean tides, so the water is salty.
Impounded wetland: a wetland where a berm or dike holds water in, which changes how often and how deeply it floods. Brackish water is in between fresh and ocean water in saltiness.

What is a flux, and what is a chamber? A flux is how much gas moves across a surface per unit area per unit time. To measure it here, researchers use chambers: closed boxes placed over the ground. Gas that leaks out of the soil and plants builds up inside the sealed space, and the rate of increase in concentration tells you the flux. A steeper rise means a larger flux. In the usual convention a positive flux is gas going from the wetland into the air (confirm this in the metadata).



A closed chamber over marsh plants and soil, with CH₄ and CO₂ entering the chamber and an inset showing concentration rising over time.


The README names three chamber types: whole-plant, plant-adjacent and non-vegetated. It does not define them, so read the metadata before you compare them. The general idea is to separate the effect of plants from the effect of bare soil. Many wetland plants can also move gas between the soil and the air through their stems, which is one reason plants matter for methane.
Soil measurements. Soil cores were taken at two depths (0–10 cm and 10–50 cm). The README lists these variables:

Carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) concentrations and the C:N ratio. C:N is the amount of carbon relative to nitrogen. It is often used as a rough sign of how easily microbes can break down the organic matter.
Moisture (how wet the soil is) and pH (how acidic or basic it is).
Conductivity: how well the soil water carries electricity. It is usually a stand-in for how salty the water is, but check the metadata.
Organic matter: the part of the soil made from once-living material.
Root biomass: the weight of roots in the soil.
mcrA gene copy numbers: mcrA is a gene that methanogens (microbes that produce methane) use. Counting its copies is a way to estimate how many methane-producing microbes are present.







Not stated in the README: the units, the exact chamber method, and how chamber and soil measurements are matched in time and place. Check the metadata page before you combine tables.

Explanation of data
The big idea. Plants take carbon dioxide (CO₂) out of the air to build their tissues, and plants and soil microbes put CO₂ back into the air when they respire. This dataset tracks that two-way traffic over a tidal salt marsh on Sapelo Island, Georgia, for about ten years. Coastal marshes like this one are often called blue carbon ecosystems because they can store carbon.
What is a flux? A flux is how much of something crosses a surface, per unit of surface area, per unit of time. Think of counting how many people walk through a doorway each minute. Here the “doorway” is the marsh surface and the “people” are CO₂ molecules, moving vertically between the marsh and the air above it.
How is it measured? Eddy covariance. Air near the ground is turbulent: it is full of small swirls called eddies that carry air up and down. An eddy covariance (EC) tower sits above the marsh with two instruments:

a sonic anemometer, which measures wind speed in three directions (including straight up or down) using sound pulses, and
a gas analyzer, which measures how much CO₂ is in the air.

If upward-moving air tends to carry more CO₂ than downward-moving air, the marsh is releasing CO₂. If upward air carries less, the marsh is taking CO₂ up. The statistical link between vertical wind and CO₂ is called a covariance, which is where the method gets its name. The tower mostly “sees” the marsh upwind of it, called the footprint. The README says the dataset records what fraction of the footprint was tall, medium or short marsh habitat (it does not define those height classes here, so check the metadata page).



An eddy covariance tower: a sonic anemometer and a gas analyzer near the top, with swirling eddies carrying CO₂ up from and down to the marsh.


NEE, GPP and ER (Reco). The three headline variables fit together like a bank account:

GPP (gross primary production) is the total CO₂ the plants pull in through photosynthesis. It is like your gross paycheck.
ER (ecosystem respiration, also written Reco) is the CO₂ released by plants and soil microbes. It is like your spending.
NEE (net ecosystem exchange) is the net result that the tower actually sees: NEE = ER − GPP (with GPP written as a positive number). It is like your balance change.

Sign convention. In this convention, a negative NEE means the ecosystem is taking up CO₂ (a sink), and a positive NEE means it is releasing CO₂ (a source). Some datasets flip the sign, so confirm it on the metadata page before you interpret a graph.



Carbon flux diagram: CO₂ goes into the plants as GPP and out as ER; NEE = ER − GPP.


Good to know: a tower measures NEE directly. GPP and ER are not measured directly. They are estimated by splitting NEE into two pieces, a step called flux partitioning. That is why the README suggests comparing methods.
Daily and seasonal cycles. A diurnal cycle is a pattern that repeats every 24 hours. At night there is no sunlight, so there is no photosynthesis and respiration dominates (NEE is positive). In daylight, photosynthesis usually rises and can outweigh respiration (NEE dips negative). A seasonal cycle is the same idea across the year: in many ecosystems uptake is strongest in the growing season. The 30-minute data let you see the daily cycle, while the daily and annual data let you see seasons and yearly totals. Check which pattern your own data actually show.



Schematic of a typical diurnal NEE cycle: slightly positive at night, negative around midday.


Gaps and uncertainty. Towers sometimes miss data (power loss, bad weather, instrument problems). Gap-filling means estimating values for the missing periods. The README mentions comparing gap-filled with observed periods, so look for a column or flag that tells them apart. The dataset also gives 95% confidence intervals, a range that very likely contains the true value, as an estimate of uncertainty.
Supporting variables. The README lists air temperature, humidity, VPD and water-table height. Relative humidity is how much water vapor is in the air compared with the most it could hold at that temperature. VPD (vapor pressure deficit) is the gap between those two amounts, so it measures how “thirsty” the air is. Water-table height is the level of the water relative to the ground. On a tidal marsh it may be linked to the tides, but the README does not say, so check the metadata.






Not stated in the README: the units of NEE, GPP and ER, the exact variable names, and the sign convention used here. Those details are on the metadata page. Eddy covariance fluxes are commonly reported as an amount of CO₂ (or carbon) per area per time, but confirm before you plot.

title: MacroSheds: Synthesis of Long-Term Biogeochemical, Hydroclimatic, and Geospatial Data from Small Watersheds
text:
What it is
A harmonized synthesis of daily streamflow, stream chemistry, precipitation, and watershed attributes from >200 small watersheds across LTER, CZO/CZNet, NEON, and other networks.

title: MacroSheds: Synthesis of Long-Term Biogeochemical, Hydroclimatic, and Geospatial Data from Small Watersheds
text:
Explanation of data
The big idea. A watershed is all the land that drains to one point on a stream, like a bowl that funnels rain to a single drain. MacroSheds gathers measurements from more than 200 small watersheds across the United States and puts them in one consistent format (the README calls this harmonized). The data come from several research networks: LTER (Long Term Ecological Research), CZO/CZNet (Critical Zone Observatories) and NEON (National Ecological Observatory Network).
What is in it? For each watershed you can find:

Discharge: how much water flows past a point in the stream per unit of time. The README says this is daily.
Solutes and chemistry: substances dissolved in the water, such as ions and nutrients (the README says “multiple ions and nutrients”).
Precipitation and precipitation chemistry where available.
Watershed attributes: facts about the land, such as climate, geology, terrain, vegetation and land cover. The README says they are aligned with CAMELS-style predictors, meaning they follow the format of a well-known set of watershed descriptors.

Concentration versus load. A concentration is how much of a dissolved substance is in a given volume of water, like how strong a drink is. A load (also called export or flux) is how much of that substance leaves the watershed over a period of time. Load depends on both concentration and discharge: a strong drink in a tiny cup carries less than a weak drink in a huge bucket. Dividing the load by watershed area gives a yield, which lets you compare large and small watersheds fairly. The README suggests studying nutrient export or retention: export is what leaves in the stream, and retention is what the watershed holds back (for example in plants and soil).



Concentration times discharge equals load; load divided by watershed area equals yield.


Weathering. The README also mentions weathering rates. Weathering is the slow breakdown of rock, which releases dissolved ions into water, so stream chemistry can carry a fingerprint of the local geology.
How to start. Because the dataset is large and varies by site (time spans differ by watershed), the README points to an R package and a dashboard that make it easier to pick sites and download them. Start with a few watersheds rather than all 200.






Not stated in the README: which specific solutes are included, the units, and which watersheds have the longest records. Use the metadata page, the dashboard and the data paper for details.

What it is
High-resolution (90 m) downscaled climate grids for California covering a variety of bioclimatic variables derived from historical climate data (1971–2000 normal period).

title: Downscaled Climate Grids of California (90 m) for Bioclimatic Variables, 1971–2000
text:
Explanation of data
The big idea. Climate is usually measured at weather stations, which are single points on a map. To study climate across a whole state you need values everywhere. This dataset gives you that as a grid: California is divided into square cells, each 90 m on a side, and every cell has a value for each climate variable. Think of a photo made of pixels, where each pixel stores a temperature or a rainfall amount instead of a color.
What does “downscaled” mean? Large-scale climate data often come in coarse cells many kilometers wide. Downscaling uses extra information, such as terrain or station measurements, to estimate climate at a finer scale, so you can tell the cool valley floor from the sunny ridge. The README does not describe the downscaling method, so see the metadata for how it was done.



Downscaling: a few coarse cells become many finer cells that show more local detail.


Bioclimatic variables. The README says the grids contain bioclimatic variables: temperature, precipitation and derived indices (numbers computed from the basic ones). Bioclimatic variables are summaries designed to matter for living things, for example the average yearly temperature, how much it rains in the driest part of the year, or how much the temperature varies through the year. These are examples of the idea: the exact list of variables is on the metadata page.
A climate normal. The README gives the period 1971–2000. A climate normal is the average over 30 years, so this dataset describes “typical” historical California climate, not a single year. It is a snapshot in time, not a time series, so questions about year-to-year change or trends do not fit this dataset.
Historical, not projected. The README describes historical data, so this dataset is not a future projection. (Some downscaled climate datasets are built from global climate models, or GCMs, which simulate Earth’s climate, and from scenarios of future emissions. Check the metadata for what was used here; the README does not say.)
Working with gridded data. Gridded data is not a normal spreadsheet. It often comes as raster files, which are images where each cell holds a value, and you need an R package that reads rasters to load it (the README does not state the file format; check before you commit). You can convert a raster to a table with one row per cell, which is useful because a project needs at least 50 rows and 10 variables. Cells that are next to each other tend to be similar, which matters when you apply statistics that assume independent observations.






Not stated in the README: the file format, the list of variables, the units and the DOI (the README says to check the metadata page).

What it is
Long-term meteorological observations from the Kellogg Biological Station LTER site in southwest Michigan. Includes both raw hourly data and quality-controlled daily and annual summaries.

title: LTER Meteorological Stations at the Kellogg Biological Station, Michigan (1941–present)
text:
Explanation of data
The big idea. This is a weather station record from the Kellogg Biological Station (KBS), an agricultural research site in southwest Michigan that belongs to the LTER (Long Term Ecological Research) network. Weather is what the atmosphere does on a given day. Climate is the long-term pattern of weather, usually judged over decades. A record that starts in 1941 is long enough to look at climate, not just weather.
What was measured? The README lists these variables:

Air temperature and precipitation (rain and melted snow).
Wind speed and direction. By meteorology’s usual convention, wind direction is where the wind blows from; confirm in the metadata.
Solar radiation: the amount of energy arriving from the sun.
Relative humidity: how much water vapor is in the air compared with the most the air could hold at that temperature, as a percentage.
Soil temperature and soil moisture.

Different time scales. The README says you get raw hourly data plus quality-controlled daily and annual summaries. A summary squeezes many measurements into one number, such as a daily average or a daily total (average for temperature, total for precipitation is the usual choice, but check the metadata). Quality-controlled means someone has checked the values for obvious errors. Hourly data is good for daily cycles; daily and annual data are better for long-term trends.
Gaps and “synthetic” records. The README says some records are synthetic complete records supplemented from nearby stations when needed. That means gaps in the KBS record were filled using data from other stations. When you analyze trends, remember that some values are estimates and look for columns that tell you which is which.
Record quality changes over time. The README says the record starts in 1941 but is most complete from 1988 onward. Be careful with trends that cross from sparse to complete years: a change could be real or could be caused by differences in how the data were collected.
Extremes. The README suggests studying extreme precipitation or heat events. An extreme is an unusually large value compared with the rest of the record (for example, a very rainy day). You can define one with a threshold, such as the top 1% of days, and then count how often it happens over time.

title: Prospect Hill Hydrological Stations at Harvard Forest (since 2005)
text:
What it is
Long-term hydrologic measurements on two small watersheds in the Prospect Hill Tract of the Harvard Forest, Massachusetts. Includes continuous automated stream and wetland water-level and discharge data.

title: Prospect Hill Hydrological Stations at Harvard Forest (since 2005)
text:
Explanation of data
The big idea. These data track how water moves through two small watersheds in the Prospect Hill Tract of Harvard Forest, Massachusetts, since 2005. (A watershed is all the land that drains to one point on a stream.) The README says the two watersheds contain contrasting wetland types: a spruce-hemlock wetland (a wet area with evergreen trees) and a beaver swamp (a wetland that formed behind a beaver dam). These are headwater wetlands, found near the start of a stream. They are interesting because wetlands can store water and release it slowly, which can smooth out the rise and fall of the stream.
What was measured? The README lists streamflow and water-level data from weirs and pipes.

Water level (stage) is the height of the water. A weir is a small dam with a known shape; the height of water behind it tells you how much is flowing over it.
Discharge (streamflow) is how much water passes a point per unit of time. It is calculated from the water level.




A weir: stage (water level) behind a small dam is converted to discharge.


Continuous, automated data. The README calls the measurements continuous automated and says there are near-real-time updates. So the record is dense and can still be growing, and the end date of your copy depends on when you download it. Check how often values are recorded (the README does not say).
Storms and seasons. The README suggests event-based or seasonal analysis. An event is a storm, and the stream’s response to it is shown on a graph called a hydrograph: flow rises as water arrives, peaks, and then slowly falls (the recession). Comparing the two watersheds’ hydrographs for the same storm shows how their wetlands and landscapes affect the response. A seasonal analysis compares wet and dry parts of the year.
Comparing two sites. The README describes the watersheds as having different topography (shape of the land) and history. When you compare them, remember that differences could come from the wetland type, the size, the slope or the land history, so say what you can and cannot conclude.

title: Interior Alaska: Climate and Wildfire Effects on Permafrost Soil Temperature Regimes (Hourly Data, 2013–2018)
text:
What it is
Hourly soil temperature measurements at depths from 5 to 150 cm at paired burned and unburned sites in Interior Alaska. Designed to examine the effects of climate and wildfire on near-surface permafrost thermal regimes.

title: Interior Alaska: Climate and Wildfire Effects on Permafrost Soil Temperature Regimes (Hourly Data, 2013–2018)
text:
Explanation of data
The big idea. Wildfire can burn trees and the organic layer (moss and partly decayed plants) on the forest floor. That organic layer works like a blanket that insulates the ground. Researchers want to know how losing it, along with climate, changes the temperature of the soil and the permafrost underneath. Permafrost is ground that stays at or below 0 °C for at least two years in a row. Above it is the active layer, the top layer that thaws in summer and refreezes in winter.



Paired unburned and burned sites with sensors at several depths in each soil column, showing the organic layer, mineral soil, the active layer and the permafrost table.


How the study is designed. The README describes paired burned and unburned sites. Paired means each burned site has a nearby unburned comparison site, so that differences are more likely to be due to the fire than to differences in the landscape. This is a common way to study an effect when you cannot run a controlled experiment. The README says the data are hourly soil temperatures at depths from 5 to 150 cm, from 2013 to 2018, in Interior Alaska. That is a time series at many depths: one set of columns per depth, or one row per depth and time, so check how your data file is organized.
What do you compare? The README suggests three ideas:

Temperature profiles at burned vs. unburned sites: compare temperature versus depth for the same date or season.
Freeze–thaw dynamics: freeze–thaw is the seasonal change between frozen and thawed soil. You can see it when soil temperature at a given depth crosses 0 °C.
Depth-dependent warming rates: does the soil warm faster near the surface or deeper down, and does that differ between burned and unburned sites?

What the README does not tell you. It does not say how severe each fire was (burn severity is how much of the vegetation and organic layer was consumed), how long ago each site burned, or what the units are (temperature is almost certainly in degrees Celsius, but verify). Do not assume the burned sites are warmer or colder: test it with the data.
Hourly data. With one record per hour, there are 24 per day, which is a lot of data. Plan whether to average to daily values (for example, daily mean at each depth) so that graphs are readable.






Not stated in the README: units, site locations, burn severity and years since fire. Check the metadata page.
